title: Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention and Treasury Data Access Act
official_title: To establish governmentwide requirements for pre-payment fraud prevention actions, to provide the U.S. Treasury appropriate data resources, to facilitate participation in governmentwide anti-fraud data sharing, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Comer (R-KY) with 3 cosponsors; passed the House. Payment-integrity measures often draw bipartisan support, but the broadened Do Not Pay data-sharing and computer-matching authority may draw privacy scrutiny, and Senate passage requires 60 votes.
summary: Builds new fraud checks into the federal payment process: before the Treasury pays out money, agencies would have to verify the payee, the amount, and the bank account, and the Treasury's 'Do Not Pay' screening system would gain explicit statutory footing and a clarified framework for the data assets it can use to screen payments.
brief: Adds governmentwide pre-payment fraud checks and puts the Treasury's Do Not Pay system on statutory footing.

top_lines.headline: Checks Before the Government Pays
subs: Agencies must clear pre-certification checks before certifying a payment voucher
Verify payee identity, amount, fund availability, and that the payee is not deceased
Confirm the bank account on the voucher belongs to the payee

top_lines.headline: Do Not Pay System in Statute
subs: Gives the Treasury-run Do Not Pay system explicit statutory authority
Treasury must publish a System of Records Notice for each data asset before it can be disclosed
Up to a $250,000 fine and 5 years in prison for unlawful disclosure

top_lines.headline: First-Time Recipient Reporting
subs: First-time recipients of awards of $50,000 or more file a one-time use-of-funds report
Noncompliance halts further payments to the recipient until the report is filed
Most provisions take effect 180 days after enactment

items.main: Names the Act the “Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention and Treasury Data Access Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention Requirements for Agencies

items.main: Bars agencies from certifying a payment voucher until a set of pre-certification checks is met.
items.detail: Adds a new section 3325a to title 31, U.S. Code. An agency head may not certify a voucher under section 3325 until pre-certification requirements are met, and the Treasury must issue implementing regulations within 180 days. The checks include confirming funds are available, the amount and payee name are correct, a valid Social Security, taxpayer, employer, or individual taxpayer identification number is provided, the appropriation is available with the correct Treasury Account Symbol, the payee is not deceased, and the account belongs to the payee. Disbursing officials must verify bank-account accuracy to the extent practicable. It also renames the Do Not Pay 'Initiative' as a 'System' and defines a 'fraud-risk indicator.'

sections.label: Section 3 — Treasury Do Not Pay System

items.main: Puts the Do Not Pay system in statute and restructures how the Treasury accesses and shares the data it uses to screen payments.
items.detail: Amends section 3354 of title 31 so each executive agency screens all recipients of federal awards or payments against Do Not Pay data assets before an award or payment. The Secretary has access to the system's data assets consistent with the routine-use authority under section 552a of title 5, and must publish a System of Records Notice identifying each data asset before it may be disclosed. The Secretary may designate additional data-asset categories after at least 15 days of public notice, and at least 30 days before adding a specific asset within a category; such data comparisons are not treated as a Privacy Act 'matching program' when the query returns a binary response, results are not retained more than 30 days, and no more than 20 record requests are made at a time; use is limited to improper-payment and law-enforcement purposes; and unlawful disclosure carries a fine of not more than $250,000, imprisonment of not more than 5 years, or both. State, local, judicial, and legislative entities get access, and the Treasury must file quarterly reports to Congress plus an annual evaluation of the system's effectiveness.

sections.label: Section 4 — Single Report on First-Time Use of Funds

items.main: Requires first-time recipients of larger federal awards to file a one-time report on how they used the money.
items.detail: Adds section 6107 to title 31. A 'covered recipient' — an entity receiving a 'covered award' (a federal award of not less than $50,000 in fiscal year 2027 constant dollars) from a program for the first time — must submit a one-time use-of-funds report within 180 days. OMB must issue governmentwide content and format rules within 1 year, updated at least every 5 years. Noncompliance triggers written notice and a halt to further disbursements until the report is filed, and reports are kept on file for at least 5 years.

items.main: Sets the effective date 180 days after enactment.
items.detail: The Act and its amendments take effect on the date that is 180 days after the date of enactment.

underreported: Agencies that adopt Treasury's standard computer-matching agreement template are deemed to satisfy the Privacy Act's matching requirements without review by a Data Integrity Board.
gaps: Agencies may request exemptions from some or all payment-verification requirements — subject to providing a plan and reasonable timeframe to remediate the need — and the bill leaves the detailed scope to Treasury guidance.
The bill treats Do Not Pay data comparisons as outside the Privacy Act's 'matching program' protections while still requiring some privacy notices.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Subramanyam
featured_quotes.text: I also rise in support of H.R. 8463, the Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention and Treasury Data Access Act. This bill will help prevent improper payments by requiring that agencies verify with the U.S. Treasury that payments are going to the right place before they are made. Agencies would be required to use the Treasury's Do Not Pay system to confirm that recipients, one, have a valid Social Security number; two, are not deceased; and, three, have a valid bank account. The bill would also impose heavy fines for any misuse of the Do Not Pay system.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Comer
featured_quotes.text: Every year, the Federal Government loses hundreds of billions of dollars to fraud and improper payments. The Government Accountability Office estimates that the Federal Government has lost over $2.8 trillion since 2003 to payments that should never have been made or were made incorrectly. Annual improper payments ballooned to nearly $236 billion in fiscal year 2023, more than six times the amount in 2003.

added: A new pre-payment certification step (31 U.S.C. 3325a) with identity, amount, and bank-account checks; a one-time first-use-of-funds report for first-time recipients of awards of $50,000 or more
modified: The Do Not Pay 'Initiative' becomes a statutory Do Not Pay 'System' run by the Treasury's Fiscal Service, with authority to designate additional data assets, a use limitation, and a disclosure penalty

added: New voluntary expedited computer-matching process — agencies adopting a standard OMB/Treasury template are deemed to satisfy Privacy Act 552a(o) without Data Integrity Board review; agreements capped at under 5 years
New System of Records Notice requirement — Treasury must publish a SORN identifying each data asset and its routine uses before any data asset may be disclosed from the Do Not Pay system
New 'data matching is not a matching program' safe harbor conditions added — binary response, results not retained over 30 days, max 20 record requests at a time
New limitation-on-use safeguards — match queries return only confirm/deny plus confidence and sources; no adverse action on the data alone; independent verification required before adverse action
New Confidentiality Maintenance paragraph requiring Treasury to preserve each data asset's source-law confidentiality level
New annual Evaluation by the agency Evaluation Officer (under section 313 of title 5) estimating fraud/improper-payment reductions and dollar savings
modified: Penalty for unlawful disclosure raised from a fine of not more than $5,000 to not more than $250,000 (imprisonment stays not more than 5 years)
Do Not Pay reporting changed from an annual report to quarterly reports to the appropriate committees
Public comment period before designating sensitive data assets shortened from not less than 30 days to not less than 15 days
Report retention period in section 3354(d) extended — '3 years' struck and replaced with '5 years' in two places
Exemption process now requires the agency to provide a plan and reasonable timeframe to remediate the need for the exemption
Section 3354 data-asset access reframed from a 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' override to access 'consistent with the routine use authority under section 552a of title 5'
State/local government provision changed from a duty to 'establish and maintain' procedures to access granted 'if procedures are established'
removed: Entire Sec. 5 'U.S. Treasury Data Access for Purposes of Program Integrity' removed — dropping new access to the National Directory of New Hires, IRS section 6103(i)(9) return-information disclosure, and new SSA section 235 verification
Section 3354 data assets G (National Directory of New Hires), H (IRS 6103(i)(9) info), and I (SSA section 235 info) that the introduced version added were removed
